items.title: The discovery authority's AI verdict: AI-moderated real interviews yes, synthetic users no
items.why: After shipping her first AI product (the Interview Coach), Teresa Torres is separating the discovery hype from the real unlock: AI can moderate and scale interviews with actual customers, but synthetic users and autogenerated personas hand you confident, wrong answers. If your team is being sold 'talk to AI personas instead of customers,' this is the credible counterweight from the person who literally wrote Continuous Discovery Habits.

items.title: Connectors can now ship interactive UI in the chat, not just text
items.why: The 2026-07-28 MCP spec release candidate makes Apps and Tasks core versioned extensions, and Claude just expanded support: a tool can now render an interactive HTML view inline — a dashboard, an editable design, live data — in a sandboxed iframe instead of returning a wall of text. This quietly changes what 'an integration' is; your AI feature's surface can live inside the assistant, so spec the UI, not just the API call.

items.title: Enterprise AI agents are shipping as staffed projects, not self-serve products
items.why: OpenAI's Presence (July 22) puts agents on real customer workflows — billing disputes, insurance claims, IT tickets — with policies, guardrails, and a human in the escalation path, delivered by forward-deployed engineers rather than as self-serve. The signal for PMs: the credible pattern for production, customer-facing agents right now is a narrow first job plus guardrails plus human escalation, not 'autonomous and self-serve.'

items.title: A narrow single-purpose Claude Skill beats a general writing assistant
items.why: Peter Yang open-sourced /no-ai-slop (July 22): one Claude Skill that strips 20+ AI-slop patterns while explaining each edit and keeping your voice — and it can trigger your own doc templates for strategy briefs and PRDs. The lesson for PMs isn't the skill, it's the shape: build tight, single-job skills that encode your standards instead of one catch-all prompt.

items.title: Computer-use agents now do your mobile QA and persona research hands-free
items.why: In Claire Vo's How I AI walkthrough, Codex's browser + computer use exhaustively QAs an onboarding flow on mobile and impersonates personas to surface friction — work PMs used to do by hand or wait on eng for. Computer use crossed from demo to daily driver this month; worth an hour pointing it at your own flow.

items.title: An agent that reads your week of Slack, Notion, and Gmail and ranks the signal
items.why: Alex Lieberman's 'Content Machine' on How I AI leads with an Oracle that scans seven days of Slack, Notion, Gmail, and meeting notes and surfaces 15 ranked spikes daily; drafts then pass a six-persona 'Writer's Council' that scores and revises until it clears a bar. Both patterns — a standing signal-aggregator and a scored review loop — port straight to PM triage and doc review.

items.title: An 'agent harness' is just code around an agent — and it beats open-ended prompting for repeat work
items.why: Claire Vo strips the jargon: a harness is a few files of code that give an agent fixed tools, encoded permissions, and a consistent output — hers runs Sentry bug triage the same way every time. Her shift in thinking: general agents like Claude Code should orchestrate specialized harnesses, not do every job from an open chat box.

items.title: ChatGPT Work: OpenAI's agent now ships finished docs, decks, and web apps
items.why: OpenAI merged Codex into ChatGPT (July 9): give it a goal and it works across your apps and files for hours, returning finished spreadsheets, decks, and web apps — rolling out to all plans. Anthropic moved Cowork to cloud and mobile the same week. Expect stakeholders to arrive with agent-built artifacts.

items.title: Hybrid agent loops: cheap local models do the volume, frontier models do the judgment
items.why: Alex Finn's 24/7 setup on How I AI: a local model scans code every 20 minutes and dumps findings to markdown; Claude Code reads the file daily and decides what's real. Running the frontier model continuously would cost thousands a month — matching model cost to task judgment is what makes always-on loops economically viable.

items.title: Gusto shipped a product line in 10 weeks: no Jira, no docs, one Zoom room
items.why: Gusto's CTO put five people, Claude Code, and a 24/7 Zoom room on a new product line and threw out the standard development process entirely. Strong teams are quietly testing how much PM scaffolding (tickets, specs, standups) agents make optional.

items.title: Inside OpenAI: PMs run Slack-triggered automations and imagegen prototypes on Codex
items.why: Peter Yang got OpenAI PM Rohan Varma to walk through his actual Codex product workflows — prototyping with image gen, kicking off automations from Slack. A rare look at how PMs inside a frontier lab do daily product work, and most of it is copyable.

items.title: Build a personal model benchmark — stop vibe-checking new releases
items.why: Claire Vo built a repeatable 'How I AI Bench' in Claude Code that scores each new model on her real tasks (PRDs, prototypes) — and the leaderboard surprised her. With a major model dropping monthly, a personal bench answers 'should I switch?' in an hour instead of a week of vibes.

items.title: Goal-based agent loops: set the outcome, let the agent prompt itself
items.why: How I AI's walkthrough builds two autonomous loops — a scheduled PR-manager in Claude Code and a Codex automation that proposes new agent skills weekly. The shift: stop prompting steps, define a validated outcome and let the agent iterate until it's met.

items.title: Context libraries: many small files beat one big brief
items.why: Teresa Torres's system: dozens of tiny, focused markdown context files with an index, loaded per-task — because too much irrelevant context makes AI worse. End each session with "what did you learn today that we should document?" and the library compounds.

items.title: Evals are the new analytics — an AI-PM core skill
items.why: Aakash Gupta's line: you can't PM an AI product without evals, the same way you can't PM without analytics. If your product grows an AI feature this year, writing evals lands on you — few PMs are ready.
